title: Project structure
text: repository follows research compendium convention (Marwick, Boettiger Mullen 2018, https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2017.1375986): installable R package holds reusable, tested methods, separate analysis/ directory uses package produce research outputs.

utils-checks.R          Internal input validation (rdsc_error_input) ├── man/                        Reference documentation (generated by roxygen2) ├── tests/testthat/             Unit, reference-agreement and simulation-property tests ├── vignettes/                  Long-form articles (built by R CMD check and pkgdown) ├── inst/CITATION title: Honest model evaluation
text: generate outcome pure noise offer 30 candidate models, using single noise predictor. Every candidate’s true --sample RMSE sd(y)=1\mathrm{sd}(y) = 1 little worse, fitting noise. common practice cross-validate candidate, pick best, report CV score. nested_cv() computes “naive” number alongside nested estimate, selection repeated inside every outer training set (Varma Simon 2006; Cawley Talbot 2010): naive estimate lower (better) nested one. even lower sample standard deviation yy, .e. error simply predicting mean. selection bias work. nested procedure, outer folds also disagree predictor “best”, sign candidate really better others: Averaged many data sets, optimism naive estimate consistently positive; package tests check .
code: set.seed(1) n <- 60 p <- 30 noise <- as.data.frame(matrix(rnorm(n * (p + 1)), n)) names(noise) <- c("y", paste0("x", seq_len(p)))  candidates <- lapply(paste0("x", seq_len(p)), function(v) {   f <- stats::as.formula(paste("y ~", v))   function(train) lm(f, data = train) }) names(candidates) <- paste0("x", seq_len(p)) ncv <- nested_cv(noise, candidates, outcome = "y", outer_k = 5, inner_k = 5,                  seed = 42) ncv #> Nested cross-validation (5 outer x 5 inner folds) #>   nested estimate = 0.8556 (SE 0.08951) #>   naive estimate  = 0.8189 (best candidate: x21) #>   pooled: nested = 0.8741, naive = 0.8431 #>   selected in outer folds: x15 (1), x30 (4) ncv$outer #>      fold n_test selected inner_score outer_score #> x30     1     12      x30   0.8435081   0.5795351 #> x301    2     12      x30   0.8310504   0.8068055 #> x15     3     12      x15   0.7111221   1.1358079 #> x302    4     12      x30   0.7942880   0.9105929 #> x303    5     12      x30   0.7846426   0.8450718

title: Honest model evaluation
text: cross_validate() takes whole modelling procedure function. step learns data, screening predictors, scaling imputing, must go inside re-learned training fold. , “leaky” version screens predictors full data set cross-validating. “honest” version screens inside fold. honest estimate correctly shows procedure better predicting mean. naive standard error printed cross_validate() treats folds independent. underestimates real uncertainty read lower bound (Bates et al. 2024).
code: screen_fit <- function(train, k = 3) {   r <- abs(cor(train[-1], train$y))[, 1]   keep <- names(sort(r, decreasing = TRUE))[seq_len(k)]   lm(stats::reformulate(keep, "y"), data = train) }  honest <- cross_validate(noise, screen_fit, outcome = "y", k = 5,                          repeats = 5, seed = 7)  r_full <- abs(cor(noise[-1], noise$y))[, 1] keep_full <- names(sort(r_full, decreasing = TRUE))[1:3] leaky <- cross_validate(   noise, function(train) lm(stats::reformulate(keep_full, "y"), data = train),   outcome = "y", k = 5, repeats = 5, seed = 7 )  c(honest = honest$estimate, leaky = leaky$estimate, sd_y = sd(noise$y)) #>    honest     leaky      sd_y  #> 0.9088186 0.7961808 0.8551688

title: Honest model evaluation
text: probabilistic classifiers, report measure discrimination (AUC) together calibration (Van Calster et al. 2019) proper scoring rule (Gneiting Raftery 2007). simulate logistic model known risks compare correctly specified model -fitted one 25 extra noise predictors. -fitted model loses discrimination, calibration far worse: -fitted model’s calibration slope well 1, meaning predictions extreme. Even correctly specified model, fitted 300 observations, slope 1: -fitting unavoidable sample size, shrinkage methods exist. AUC measures well cases ranked, reveal badly probabilities miscalibrated. Brier score log loss, proper scoring rules, .
code: train <- simulate_logistic(300, beta = c(1, -0.8, 0.5, rep(0, 25)),                            intercept = -0.5, seed = 11) test <- simulate_logistic(5000, beta = c(1, -0.8, 0.5, rep(0, 25)),                           intercept = -0.5, seed = 12)  small <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = train, family = binomial) big <- glm(y ~ . - p, data = train, family = binomial)  p_small <- predict(small, test, type = "response") p_big <- predict(big, test, type = "response")  rbind(   small = auc_ci(test$y, p_small),   big = auc_ci(test$y, p_big) ) #>             auc          se     lower     upper level n_pos n_neg #> small 0.7953547 0.006317031 0.7826952 0.8074581  0.95  2030  2970 #> big   0.7577897 0.006808942 0.7441956 0.7708838  0.95  2030  2970 rbind(small = calibration(test$y, p_small)[2, ],       big = calibration(test$y, p_big)[2, ]) #>       parameter  estimate         se     lower     upper #> small     slope 0.8271002 0.02677777 0.7746167 0.8795836 #> big       slope 0.5053267 0.01810925 0.4698332 0.5408202 c(brier_small = brier_score(test$y, p_small),   brier_big = brier_score(test$y, p_big),   logloss_small = log_loss(test$y, p_small),   logloss_big = log_loss(test$y, p_big)) #>   brier_small     brier_big logloss_small   logloss_big  #>     0.1838224     0.2114921     0.5469129     0.6412775 bin_cal <- function(y, p, bins = 10) {   g <- cut(p, stats::quantile(p, seq(0, 1, length.out = bins + 1)),            include.lowest = TRUE)   data.frame(pred = tapply(p, g, mean), obs = tapply(y, g, mean)) } cs <- bin_cal(test$y, p_small) cb <- bin_cal(test$y, p_big) plot(cs$pred, cs$obs, pch = 19, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1),      xlab = "Mean predicted risk", ylab = "Observed event rate") points(cb$pred, cb$obs, pch = 17, col = 2) abline(0, 1, lty = 2) legend("topleft", c("correct model", "over-fitted"), pch = c(19, 17),        col = 1:2, bty = "n")

title: Resampling inference and effect sizes
text: Consider ratio mean fuel consumption automatic manual cars mtcars. ratio simple standard error, nonparametric bootstrap gives one directly. statistic data frame, boot_ci() resamples rows. four methods rest different assumptions (Davison Hinkley 1997): percentile: quantiles bootstrap distribution. transformation-respecting first-order accurate. basic: reflects percentile interval around estimate. normal: estimate minus bootstrap bias, plus minus normal quantile times bootstrap SE. BCa: corrects percentile interval median bias (ẑ0\hat z_0) skewness via acceleration ̂\hat (Efron 1987). second-order accurate usually preferred.  boot_ci() reproduces boot::boot.ci() machine precision given seed (see package tests). adds small, validated interface guarantee caller’s random number stream changed.
code: ratio <- function(d) mean(d$mpg[d$am == 0]) / mean(d$mpg[d$am == 1]) ci <- boot_ci(mtcars, ratio, R = 1999, seed = 2024) ci #> Nonparametric bootstrap confidence intervals #> n = 32, R = 1999 replicates #>  #> Estimate: 0.703  (bias 0.002727, SE 0.05936) #>  #>        type level  lower  upper #>  percentile   95% 0.5996 0.8215 #>       basic   95% 0.5845 0.8063 #>      normal   95% 0.5839 0.8166 #>         bca   95% 0.5961 0.8165 c(bias_correction = ci$bias_correction, acceleration = ci$acceleration) #> bias_correction    acceleration  #>    -0.038254532    -0.003122252 hist(ci$replicates, breaks = 40, main = "Bootstrap distribution",      xlab = "ratio of means", col = "grey85", border = "white") abline(v = ci$estimate, lwd = 2)

title: Resampling inference and effect sizes
text: permutation test gives exact test null hypothesis group labels exchangeable. 13 manual 19 automatic cars (3213)≈3.5×108\binom{32}{13} \approx 3.5 \times 10^{8} rearrangements, far many enumerate, perm_test() draws random sample : p-value computed (b+1)/(R+1)(b + 1)/(R + 1), never b/Rb/R. b/Rb/R estimator can return zero, test built anti-conservative (Phipson Smyth 2010). statistic can used, difference medians: reference set small, test exact. paired sleep data 210=10242^{10} = 1024 sign flips:
code: manual <- mtcars$mpg[mtcars$am == 1] auto <- mtcars$mpg[mtcars$am == 0] pt <- perm_test(manual, auto, R = 9999, seed = 1) pt #>  #>  Monte Carlo two-sample permutation test #>  #> data:  manual and auto #> T = 7.2449, rearrangements = 9999, p-value = 3e-04 #> alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0 pt$p.value.mcse #> [1] 0.0001731878 perm_test(manual, auto, statistic = function(x, y) median(x) - median(y),           R = 9999, seed = 1)$p.value #> [1] 0.0189 perm_test(sleep$extra[1:10], sleep$extra[11:20], paired = TRUE) #>  #>  Exact paired sign-flip randomisation test #>  #> data:  sleep$extra[1:10] and sleep$extra[11:20] #> T = -1.58, rearrangements = 1024, p-value = 0.003906 #> alternative hypothesis: true location is not equal to 0

title: Resampling inference and effect sizes
text: p-value says nothing magnitude effect. Standardised mean differences , commonly reported large-sample intervals can badly wrong small samples. cohens_d() hedges_g() invert noncentral tt distribution instead (Steiger Fouladi 1997; Cumming Finch 2001): Hedges’ gg applies exact correction J(ν)J(\nu), removes upward bias dd small samples (Hedges 1981):

title: Designing and reporting simulation studies
text: Student tt interval. bootstrap percentile interval. bootstrap BCa interval. bootstrap basic interval. analysis function returns one row per method:
code: analyse <- function(x) {   tt <- stats::t.test(x)   bs <- boot_ci(x, mean, R = 499, type = c("percentile", "bca", "basic"))   data.frame(     method = c("t", bs$intervals$type),     estimate = mean(x),     se = c(sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)), rep(bs$se, 3)),     lower = c(tt$conf.int[1], bs$intervals$lower),     upper = c(tt$conf.int[2], bs$intervals$upper)   ) }

text: Coverage estimates always plotted Monte Carlo uncertainty:  Three findings stand . () methods -cover skew strong, badly n=10n = 10: bootstrap intervals mean narrow small samples, partly plug-variance divides nn rather n−1n - 1(Davison Hinkley 1997). (ii) basic interval clearly worst, theory predicts skewed statistics, reflects bootstrap distribution wrong way. (iii) 500 replicates, differences tt, percentile BCa intervals mostly comparable Monte Carlo SEs, small study rank . Without MCSEs tempting -interpret differences. larger study analysis/ designed resolve .
code: perf <- sim_performance(res, true = "theta", by = c("n", "sigma", "method")) cov <- subset(perf, measure == "coverage") cov[, c("n", "sigma", "method", "estimate", "mcse")] #> Simulation performance measures (Morris et al., 2019) #>  #>   n sigma     method estimate (MCSE) #>  10   0.5      basic   0.896 (0.014) #>  40   0.5      basic   0.916 (0.012) #>  10   1.0      basic   0.752 (0.019) #>  40   1.0      basic   0.874 (0.015) #>  10   0.5        bca   0.928 (0.012) #>  40   0.5        bca   0.936 (0.011) #>  10   1.0        bca   0.814 (0.017) #>  40   1.0        bca   0.912 (0.013) #>  10   0.5 percentile   0.924 (0.012) #>  40   0.5 percentile   0.922 (0.012) #>  10   1.0 percentile   0.790 (0.018) #>  40   1.0 percentile   0.904 (0.013) #>  10   0.5          t   0.942 (0.010) #>  40   0.5          t   0.930 (0.011) #>  10   1.0          t   0.822 (0.017) #>  40   1.0          t   0.902 (0.013) cov$label <- sprintf("n=%d, sigma=%.1f", cov$n, cov$sigma) methods <- unique(cov$method) labels <- unique(cov$label) pos <- outer(seq_along(labels), (seq_along(methods) - 2.5) * 0.18, "+") plot(NA, xlim = c(0.5, length(labels) + 0.5), ylim = c(0.75, 1),      xaxt = "n", xlab = "", ylab = "Coverage") axis(1, at = seq_along(labels), labels = labels, cex.axis = 0.8) abline(h = 0.95, lty = 2) for (m in seq_along(methods)) {   d <- cov[cov$method == methods[m], ]   x <- pos[match(d$label, labels), m]   arrows(x, d$estimate - 1.96 * d$mcse, x, d$estimate + 1.96 * d$mcse,          angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.02, col = m)   points(x, d$estimate, pch = 19, col = m) } legend("bottomright", legend = methods, col = seq_along(methods), pch = 19,        bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

title: Reproducible Resampling, Simulation and Model-Evaluation Methods
code: library(RDataScienceCompendium)  # BCa bootstrap interval for a ratio of means ratio <- function(d) mean(d$mpg[d$am == 0]) / mean(d$mpg[d$am == 1]) boot_ci(mtcars, ratio, R = 1999, type = "bca", seed = 1)  # Permutation test (exact when feasible, otherwise Phipson-Smyth p-value) perm_test(mtcars$mpg[mtcars$am == 1], mtcars$mpg[mtcars$am == 0], seed = 1)  # Effect size with an exact noncentral-t interval hedges_g(mtcars$mpg[mtcars$am == 1], mtcars$mpg[mtcars$am == 0])  # A simulation study with Monte Carlo standard errors res <- run_simulation(   generate = function(n) rexp(n),   analyse  = function(x) {     ci <- t.test(x)$conf.int     c(estimate = mean(x), lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2])   },   n_sim = 2000, scenarios = data.frame(n = c(10, 40)), seed = 42 ) sim_performance(res, true = 1)  # Nested cross-validation versus the optimistic "naive" estimate candidates <- list(   wt    = function(d) lm(mpg ~ wt, data = d),   wt_hp = function(d) lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = d),   all   = function(d) lm(mpg ~ ., data = d) ) nested_cv(mtcars, candidates, outcome = "mpg", seed = 1)

title: Reproducible Resampling, Simulation and Model-Evaluation Methods
text: Design principles: Reproducible randomness. Every stochastic function takes seed restores caller’s RNG state. Simulation replicates get independent L’Ecuyer-CMRG streams, results depend number parallel workers. Honest uncertainty. Monte Carlo p-values never zero, simulation summaries always come Monte Carlo standard errors. Documented caveats stated estimators known biased, naive CV standard error. Validated, just tested. method checked independent reference: reference implementation, closed-form identity, simulation property coverage, unbiasedness type error. Minimal dependencies. base R run time; boot future optional used tests parallelism. Test coverage 97%; per-file breakdown summary test-coverage run.

title: Reproducible Resampling, Simulation and Model-Evaluation Methods
text: analysis/ holds two simulation studies designed reported ADEMP framework Morris, White Crowther (2019): Study 1: bootstrap intervals rescue small, skewed samples? Five nominal 95% intervals log-normal mean compared: tt, percentile, basic, normal BCa, 12 scenarios × 5,000 replicates coverage MCSE 0.6 points. mild moderate skew, plain tt interval -covered every bootstrap interval every nn. n=10n = 10 σ=0.25\sigma = 0.25, tt covered 94.1% bootstrap intervals covered 90%. strong skew, every method -covered (77–84% n=10n = 10). BCa best bootstrap method matched beat tt n=20n = 20. basic interval worst whenever skew mild. Study 2: optimistic cross-validation model selection? true test-set RMSE “select CV, refit” procedure compared naive CV estimate (best candidate’s CV score) nested CV. estimate computed averaging per-fold RMSEs pooled --fold predictions. 8 scenarios × 1,000 replicates. Naive CV understated RMSE 0.107, small nn many candidates. second, less familiar bias turned : averaging per-fold RMSEs made even nested CV optimistic, 0.017 (Jensen’s inequality). finding led cross_validate() nested_cv() also reporting pooled estimates. pooling, nested CV unbiased within 2 MCSE 6 8 scenarios. two slightly conservative (+0.021 ), expected training 80% data. full write-, tables figures, analysis/paper/paper.Rmd. rendered, self-contained version analysis/paper/paper.html. Summarised results provenance (seed, replicates, R version, platform, run time) analysis/results/.

title: Run a reproducible Monte Carlo simulation study — run_simulation
code: # Coverage of the t-interval for the mean of skewed data gen <- function(n) rexp(n) ana <- function(x) {   tt <- t.test(x)   c(estimate = mean(x), se = sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)),     lower = tt$conf.int[1], upper = tt$conf.int[2]) } res <- run_simulation(gen, ana, n_sim = 200,                       scenarios = data.frame(n = c(10, 50)), seed = 2024) sim_performance(res, true = 1) #> Simulation performance measures (Morris et al., 2019) #>  #>   n            measure estimate (MCSE) n_rep n_missing #>  10               bias  -0.016 (0.022)   200         0 #>  10       empirical_se   0.314 (0.016)   200         0 #>  10                mse   0.098 (0.011)   200         0 #>  10           model_se   0.308 (0.009)   200         0 #>  10 rel_error_model_se  -1.821 (5.767)   200         0 #>  10           coverage   0.895 (0.022)   200         0 #>  10        be_coverage   0.905 (0.021)   200         0 #>  10         mean_width   1.294 (0.037)   200         0 #>  50               bias   0.006 (0.010)   200         0 #>  50       empirical_se   0.148 (0.007)   200         0 #>  50                mse   0.022 (0.002)   200         0 #>  50           model_se   0.143 (0.002)   200         0 #>  50 rel_error_model_se  -3.502 (5.065)   200         0 #>  50           coverage   0.940 (0.017)   200         0 #>  50        be_coverage   0.940 (0.017)   200         0 #>  50         mean_width   0.563 (0.008)   200         0

what: Number of replicates needed for a target Monte Carlo standard error — sim_n_required
title: Number of replicates needed for a target Monte Carlo standard error — sim_n_required
text: Planning formulas Morris, White Crowther (2019, Section 5.3). proportions (coverage, rejection rates), \(n = p(1-p)/\mathrm{MCSE}^2\); bias, \(n = \sigma^2/\mathrm{MCSE}^2\), \(\sigma\) anticipated empirical standard error estimator.

title: Number of replicates needed for a target Monte Carlo standard error — sim_n_required
code: sim_n_required(   target_mcse,   measure = c("proportion", "bias"),   p = 0.5,   sd = NULL )

title: Number of replicates needed for a target Monte Carlo standard error — sim_n_required
text: target_mcse Desired Monte Carlo standard error. measure "proportion" (coverage, power, type error) "bias". p Anticipated proportion; 0.5 gives worst case. sd Anticipated empirical SE estimator ("bias").

title: Number of replicates needed for a target Monte Carlo standard error — sim_n_required
text: required number replicates (rounded ).

title: Number of replicates needed for a target Monte Carlo standard error — sim_n_required
code: # MCSE of 0.5 percentage points for coverage near 95% sim_n_required(0.005, p = 0.95) #> [1] 1900

what: Performance measures for a simulation study, with Monte Carlo SEs — sim_performance
title: Performance measures for a simulation study, with Monte Carlo SEs — sim_performance
text: Summarises output run_simulation() (data frame replicate-level results) using performance measures Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE) formulas Morris, White Crowther (2019, Table 6).

title: Performance measures for a simulation study, with Monte Carlo SEs — sim_performance
code: sim_performance(   results,   true,   estimate = "estimate",   se = "se",   lower = "lower",   upper = "upper",   p_value = "p_value",   alpha = 0.05,   by = NULL )

title: Performance measures for a simulation study, with Monte Carlo SEs — sim_performance
text: results data frame replicate-level results. true true value estimand: single number, name column results (estimands vary across scenarios). estimate, se, lower, upper, p_value Names columns holding point estimate, model-based standard error, confidence limits p-value. Measures whose columns absent skipped. alpha Nominal significance level rejection. Grouping columns. Defaults scenario variables recorded run_simulation() plus method column, present.

title: Performance measures for a simulation study, with Monte Carlo SEs — sim_performance
text: Morris, T. P., White, . R. Crowther, M. J. (2019). Using simulation studies evaluate statistical methods. Statistics Medicine, 38(11), 2074–2102. doi:10.1002/sim.8086

title: Performance measures for a simulation study, with Monte Carlo SEs — sim_performance
code: set.seed(1) est <- rnorm(1000, mean = 0.1, sd = 1) res <- data.frame(estimate = est, se = 1,                   lower = est - 1.96, upper = est + 1.96) sim_performance(res, true = 0) #> Simulation performance measures (Morris et al., 2019) #>  #>             measure estimate (MCSE) n_rep n_missing #>                bias   0.088 (0.033)  1000         0 #>        empirical_se   1.035 (0.023)  1000         0 #>                 mse   1.078 (0.048)  1000         0 #>            model_se   1.000 (0.000)  1000         0 #>  rel_error_model_se  -3.374 (2.162)  1000         0 #>            coverage   0.935 (0.008)  1000         0 #>         be_coverage   0.934 (0.008)  1000         0 #>          mean_width   3.920 (0.000)  1000         0

what: Simulate data with a known ground truth — simulate_data
title: Simulate data with a known ground truth — simulate_data
text: Generators linear logistic regression data correlated Gaussian predictors. true coefficients stored "truth" attribute estimators can evaluated .

title: Simulate data with a known ground truth — simulate_data
code: simulate_linear(n, beta, intercept = 0, sigma = 1, rho = 0, seed = NULL)  simulate_logistic(n, beta, intercept = 0, rho = 0, seed = NULL)  ar1_cor(p, rho)

title: Simulate data with a known ground truth — simulate_data
text: n Number observations. beta Numeric vector slope coefficients; length sets number predictors. intercept Intercept \(\beta_0\). sigma Residual standard deviation (simulate_linear() ). rho AR(1) correlation adjacent predictors, (-1, 1). seed Optional seed; caller's RNG state restored exit. p Number predictors (ar1_cor() ).

title: Simulate data with a known ground truth — simulate_data
text: data frame outcome y predictors x1, ..., xp, attribute truth (list generating parameters). simulate_logistic() true event probabilities column p.

title: Simulate data with a known ground truth — simulate_data
text: Predictors follow multivariate normal distribution unit variances first-order autoregressive correlation \(\mathrm{Cor}(X_j, X_k) = \rho^{|j-k|}\). simulate_linear(), \(Y = \beta_0 + X\beta + \varepsilon\) \(\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\). simulate_logistic(), \(Y \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}\{\mathrm{expit}(\beta_0 + X\beta)\}\).

title: Simulate data with a known ground truth — simulate_data
code: d <- simulate_linear(200, beta = c(1, 0.5, 0), sigma = 2, seed = 1) coef(lm(y ~ ., data = d)) #>  (Intercept)           x1           x2           x3  #>  0.007797159  1.009097406  0.202646350 -0.059286978  attr(d, "truth")$beta #> [1] 1.0 0.5 0.0  d2 <- simulate_logistic(500, beta = c(1, -1), intercept = -1, seed = 1) mean(d2$y) #> [1] 0.366
